n8b.vllm-i-klartext.2: The model itself can only work out the next word for one text. vLLM is the program around the model that takes questions from many users, divides the GPU’s memory between them and makes sure the GPU always has as much useful work as possible. Think of a restaurant with a single, very fast kitchen.
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.9: The maître d’ who decides who gets a table
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.12: The tables, divided into small slots
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.13: KV memory, divided into blocks of 16 tokens
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.15: The chef who cooks one bite for every table at once
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.16: The GPU running one step for the whole batch
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.18: A new table is set as soon as someone leaves
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.21: Groups that order the same starter share it
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.24: A huge order is cooked in rounds
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.30: Three things vLLM does better than a simple solution
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.31: No memory is reserved unnecessarily. Every conversation gets new memory blocks only once it needs them.
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.32: The GPU never sits waiting for a group to finish. Every step is filled with the questions that exist right then.
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.33: The same work is not done twice. Common beginnings of questions are computed once and shared.
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.34: All of this exists because the GPU, as we saw, mostly waits on memory. The more users that share each weight read, the more answers per second.
n8b.vllm-i-klartext.35: The analogy breaks down at one point: the chef does not cook a whole dish at a time but exactly one bite per table per round. That corresponds to one token per conversation and step.
